One-dimensional CuIn alloy nanowires as a robust and efficient electrocatalyst for selective CO2-to-CO conversion
Youn Jeong Janga, Jaehyuk Leeb, Ju Hun Kima, Byeong Jun Leea, Jae Sung Leea,∗
a School of Energy and Chemical Engineering, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST), Ulsan 44919 South Korea b School of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853, USA
H I G H L I G H T S
• 1-D CuIn nanowire electrocatalyst is prepared by anodization and electrodeposition. • In(OH)3 layer is formed on CuIn alloy surface by electrochemical pre-activation. • The catalyst shows best CO2–to-CO reduction activity among reported CuIn catalysts. • 1-D nanostructuring provides higher surface areas and facile charge transfer.
G R A P H I C A L A B S T R A C T
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction CuIn alloy Nanowires Selective CO production Electrocatalyst
A B S T R A C T
Electrical anodization of Cu foil produces one-dimensional Cu nanowires of high surface areas, which turns to CuIn alloy nanowires by indium electrodeposition replacing edge site Cu atoms. An electrochemical pre-activation forms a highly conformal amorphous In(OH)3 overlayer with oxygen vacancy on the CuIn alloy that facilitates CO2 adsorption to promote selective CO formation suppressing competing H2 adsorption. Thus the activated CuIn alloy nanowires catalyse electrochemical CO2 conversion to CO with high CO selectivity (> 68.2%) and high current density (ca. −3.9 mAcm−2) at −0.6 VRHE, which represents the higher partial CO current density (ca. −2.66mAcm−2) than that of previously reported CuIn alloy powders without nanostructuring. The performance remains stable for more than 15 h without significant degradation.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Re-utilization of CO2 has been a subject of immense global interest lately as a carbon-neutral technology by converting the greenhouse gas into useful fuels and chemicals instead of storage in geological or ocean reservoirs. Among diverse ways of CO2 conversion, electrocatalytic methods are effective and simple because of mild operating conditions, product versatility, and eco-friendliness. Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to CO is one of those highly desired processes because CO is a feedstock for a variety of hydrocarbons and oxygenates [1–4]. However, the technology suffers from significant challenges of low efficiency, poor
product selectivity, insufficient stability and high cost [4]. Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction has long been studied over different metal electrodes comparing their reaction rates (or overpotentials required to obtain a given current) and formed products (or selectivity) [5]. Noble metals like Ag and Au are selective for CO production, but high overpotentials and expensive prices are drawbacks [6–8]. On the other hands, Cu has many attractive characteristics for electrochemical CO2 conversion including low onset potential, low cost, and high activity of CO2 conversion. However, its low product selectivity is a disadvantage forming diverse product mixtures containing H2, CO, hydrocarbons and oxygenates [9–12].

In attempt to design noble metal-free electrocatalysts of CO2 reduction with high activity and outstanding product selectivity, metal alloy formation was suggested as an effective strategy [13–16]. Metal alloys can tune electrocatalytic properties of component metals by modifying their electronic structures and rendering ensemble or geometric effects [14,16]. An interesting example is a copper-indium (CuIn) bimetallic alloy fabricated by in-situ reduction of copper oxide followed by indium deposition reported by Takanabe and coworkers [17]. By replacing edge-site copper atoms with indium, the nature of active sites for CO2 conversion was altered. Thus, Cu edge atoms prefer the adsorption of proton in water, while indium atoms occupying edge sites of Cu adsorb CO2 preferentially. This leads to dominant CO production suppressing H2 evolution in electrocatalytic CO2 reduction on CuIn alloys. But their current density was only moderate with −0.65mAcm−2 at −0.6 VRHE. They also reported a CuIn alloy derived from CuInO2 that showed a high CO faradaic efficiency of ca. 55% at −0.6 VRHE, but a marginally improved current density of −0.8mAcm−2 [18].
Here we report one-dimensional (1-D) CuIn nanowires as an electrocatalyst for electrochemical CO2 conversion to CO with outstanding CO selectivity (> 68.2%), high current density (ca. −3.9mAcm−2 at −0.6 VRHE) and excellent stability (> 15 h), representing the best performance reported so far for electrocatalysts based on Cu-In. The 1-D nanowire morphology obtained by electrical anodization of Cu foil offers high surface areas and facile charge transfer that lead to the high current density. In particular, an electrochemical pre-activation forms a highly conformal In(OH)3 overlayer with oxygen vacancies on the CuIn alloy surface, which promotes selective CO production suppressing formation of side products like H2 and HCOOH.

sections.heading: 2.1. Electrode preparation
sections.text: Cu foil (Aldrich, 99.98%) was cleaned with acetone, ethanol, 2M HCl (Aldrich, 37–38%) and distillated water for 5min. The CuIn bimetallic alloy was prepared in two steps of anodization followed by In replacement. First, copper oxide (CuxO) nanowires were grown on cleaned Cu foil through a chronopotential anodization at 2mAcm−2 for 5min in 1M NaOH and calcination under Ar flow (100 sccm) at 200 °C for 2 h. The CuIn bimetallic alloy was prepared by a chronopotential galvanic replacement at −5mAcm−2 for 5min in an aqueous solution of 0.05M In2(SO4)3 xH2O (Aldrich, 99.99%) and 0.4M citric acid (Samchun, 98%). The Cu substrate was connected with Cu wire using Ag paste and all area except CuIn was covered by epoxy resin. For electrochemical activation, the electrode was biased at −0.6 VRHE in CO2 saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 (Junsei) for 6 h.

sections.heading: 2.2. Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction
sections.text: Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction was performed in a standard 3- electrode cell with the CuIn alloy, a Pt mesh and Ag/AgCl as working, counter, and reference electrodes, respectively. The electrolyte was CO2-saturated 0.5M KHCO3 (Wako, 99.9%) and all measurements were taken using a potentiostat (Gamry Reference 600TM). The collected gaseous reduction products in head-space (10ml) were analyzed by a gas chromatography (GC, Agilent 7890) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) connected to a Carboxen 1000 packed column, and a flame ionization detector (FID) to an Agilent Poraplot-Q capillary column. Liquid products in a cathode chamber were analyzed by a highresolution liquid chromatography (HPLC, Agilent 1200) with a C18 Inverse column. Surface roughness factors were evaluated by measuring double layer capacitances. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was conducted in the same electrolyte and the geometric current density, where no Faraday process was occurring, was plotted as a function of CV scan rate, and the linear slope yielded the capacitance.

sections.heading: 2.3. Characterization
sections.text: Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, JEOL JMS7401F), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM, Cs-corrected, JEOL JEM-2200FS) were used to obtain microscopic images of the electrodes. For TEM analysis, the CuIn alloy sample powder was obtained by grinding the surface of the electrode with a sharpener and was dispersed in absolute ethanol. X-ray diffraction spectrometry (XRD, Mac Science, M18XHF using Cu K α radiation, λ =0.15406 nm), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were applied to investigate crystallinity and oxidation state of the electrocatalyst.

sections.heading: 3. Results
sections.text:
The 1-D CuIn bimetallic nanowire electrocatalyst of a high surface area was fabricated in two steps as depicted in Fig. 1: Anodization of Cu foil and indium electrodeposition at Cu edge sites using chronopotential programs shown in Figure S1 of Supporting Information (SI). Electrochemical anodization of Cu foil at 2 mAcm−2 for 5min produces Cu (OH)2 nanowires, which are converted into CuxO nanowires through annealing at 200 °C in Ar flow. Then CuIn bimetallic alloy is fabricated by electrodeposition of indium at −5mAcm−2. X-ray diffraction (XRD) revealed the formation of CuIn alloy (JCPDS no. 00-035-1150) on Cu foil in Figure S2. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images in Figure S3 demonstrate a well-preserved nanowire morphology during the transformation of Cu(OH)2 → CuxO → CuIn.
The duration of electrodeposition step was optimized based on
generated electrochemical currents and CO selectivity with the CuIn alloy electrocatalyst as a cathode for an electrochemical CO2 reduction cell in a typical 3-electrode configuration with a Pt counter electrode and an Ag/AgCl reference electrode in a CO2-saturated 0.5M KHCO3 electrolyte. Increased duration enlarges the diameter of nanowires from ∼100 nm to ∼145 nm as shown in SEM images (Figure S4), and intensifies a peak in the early-stage of linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) around−0.2 VRHE in Figure S5, which is typically ascribed to formation of a thin indium oxide film [19,20]. In addition, the potential that produces a current of −10mAcm−2 (η10) is more negatively shifted by increasing the amount of indium due to its relatively high overpotential. A higher indium loading also increases side product formation at −0.6 VRHE. Considering generated current density and CO selectivity, CuIn alloy with 5min of indium electrodeposition was chosen as the optimized electrocatalyst. Finally, CuIn alloy was electrochemically pre-activated by chronoamperometry at −0.6 VRHE for 6 h to improve CO selectivity of the electrochemical CO2 reduction.
Fig. 2 shows high resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of pre-activated CuIn alloy nanowires (CuIn-Act). Well-developed nanowires of a high aspect ratio (∼120 nm diameter, ∼6μm length) are formed. The nanowires are polycrystalline and their diameter is highly nonuniform. Elemental maps based on TEM show that Cu and In elements are welldispersed in the CuIn-Act nanowires. A HR-TEM image of a nanowire shows that a thin amorphous In(OH)3 layer (∼5 nm) covers all the surface of catalyst almost conformally. The bulk is highly crystalline CuIn alloy showing well-defined lattice fringes of d ∼0.133 nm due to CuIn (101) planes. This amorphous In(OH)3 skin is not seen in as-prepared sample in Figure S6, indicating that it is formed during the preactivation step.
To study the effect of pre-activation, we carried out XRD and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analyses of CuIn alloy before (Figure S7) and after (Fig. 3) the pre-activation treatment for 6 h. The XRD patterns show no change in crystalline phases from those of as-prepared CuIn, showing CuIn alloy and Cu substrate in Figure S2. However, dramatic changes are observed in XPS. Even after the pre-activation, Cu XPS maintains the metallic Cu0 state, but indium XPS show both metallic In0 and In3+. As in Fig. 3d, oxygen XPS could be deconvoluted into mainly hydroxide, oxygen vacancy and metal oxide. Thus, the
electrochemical oxidation of indium starts initially to form In2O3, which is transformed into In(OH)3 with oxygen vacancy during the chronoamperometry step in aqueous solution, leading to the amorphous In(OH)3 overlayer on the CuIn surface [19–21].
Fig. 4a shows performances of electrochemical CO2 reduction in CO2-saturated 0.5M KHCO3 electrolyte for pre-activated CuIn alloy (CuIn-Act) compared with Cu foil, anodized copper oxide (CuxO), and as-prepared CuIn alloy (CuIn). Surprisingly, CuIn-Act and as-prepared CuIn alloy exhibit exactly overlapped LSV curves in the potential range of −0.8–0.0 VRHE, implying that the pre-activation does not change electron transfer characteristics or electrocatalytic activity as also shown in Figure S8. But they show a dramatic switch of main product from H2 to CO. This remarkable selectivity change by the pre-activation is a unique feature of the CuIn alloy electrocatalyst. The electrodes of polycrystalline Cu and anodized CuxO do not show such a change by the same pre-activation treatment as shown in Figure S9. The CuIn-Act electrodes show a high performance with high current density (−3.9mAcm−2 at −0.6 VRHE) and low onset potential (−0.3 VRHE) relative to Cu foil (−0.8 mAcm−2/-0.5 VRHE). On the other hands, the activity of CuxO gradually decreased with pre-activation time, indicating substantial corrosion of the catalyst itself.
The product distributions are presented as a function of applied potential in Fig. 4b. Cu foil is mainly a water reduction catalyst producing H2 dominantly at all applied potentials and begins to show CO2 reduction products from −0.6 VRHE [11]. The CuxO exhibits initially very high currents but a low overall faradaic efficiency due to self-reduction as is well known for this material [18,22]. It also produces H2 dominantly with only a minor CO production [11,17]. In contrast, asprepared CuIn alloy evolves CO over 41% with minor products of HCOOH (<8%) and H2 (< 36%) in Fig. 4b and Figure S8. The optimized CuIn-Act produces CO from CO2 with at least 55% of selectivity limiting H2 production below 25%.
To test stability of the electrocatalyst, chronoamperometry was carried out with CO2 bubbling at −0.6 VRHE for 15 h including two degassing intervals in Fig. 4c. The CuIn-Act electrode exhibits an extremely stable current density with high CO selectivity (CO faradaic efficiency > 68.2%) with minor H2 (< 11.7%) and HCOOH (< 5%) productions after initial period of product accumulation. The excellent stability of the CuIn-Act catalyst is also demonstrated in Figure S10 by showing the almost exactly superimposed LSV curves and the same morphology before and after the stability test for 15 h. During the chronoameperometry, the CuIn-Act electrode maintained the current density of ca. −3.6mAcm−2 at −0.6 VRHE. Compared with previously reported performance data for Cu-In based electrodes summarized in Table S1 [17,18,20], the partial current density of CO from our CuIn alloy nanowire electrode is the highest among previously reported CuIn alloys, but the CO faradaic efficiency is comparable.

sections.heading: 4. Discussion
sections.text:
Then what are the origins of the superior performance of our CuIn alloy electrode? First, the 1-D nanowire morphology of the CuIn alloy could be considered. The first anodization step determines the morphology of CuIn alloy as shown in Figs. 1 and 2 and its high surface area with many grain boundaries could improve the electrocatalytic activity relative to previously reported Cu-In electrocatalysts of a random particulate morphology. Indeed, roughness factor (RF) of activated CuIn alloy measured by cyclic voltammetry increases dramatically by 192.5 times relative to the pristine Cu foil as in Figure S11 [23–25]. To confirm the unique morphological effect, CuIn-Cal sample was prepared by thermal oxidation (instead of anodization) of Cu foil and galvanic indium replacement following the procedure of the previous report [17]. As shown in Figure S12, the CuIn-Act-Cal reference electrocatalyst is made of huge agglomerated particles of a random morphology and exhibits 112.5 times higher RF value than Cu foil, but still ca. two-fold lower than that of our CuIn-Act nanowires. As shown in Table S2, the
CuIn-Act-Cal electrode converts CO2 selectively into CO like our CuInAct nanowires, yet its current density is ∼4 times lower (ca. −1.0mAcm−2 at −0.6 VRHE) than that of CuIn-Act. The difference in the current density is much larger than expected from the difference in RF values (a factor of< 2). Thus, facile electron transfer along the axis the 1-D nanoscale electrocatalyst should also contribute to the superior performance in addition to the higher surface area [26].
As mentioned, alloy formation increases the activity and CO selectivity of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. To see if alloying would modify electronic structure of Cu by shifting d-band centers and thus influence binding strength of intermediates [13–16], surface valence band photoemission spectra (UPS) of electrocatalysts were studied in Figure S13. No sign of d-band shift is observed, because the completely filled d-band of indium does not influence the d-band of Cu [17].
Fig. 3. a) X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (* CuIn: JCPDS no. 00-035-1150 and ■ Cu: JCPDS no. 01-070-3039) and Xray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) of b) Cu, c) In, and d) O of pre-activated CuIn alloy (CuIn-Act).
Instead, the primary role of alloy seems to be modification of the nature of local active sites. In CuIn alloy, indium metal deposits at Cu edge sites due to an energetic preference as suggested by DFT calculation [17]. The edge sites of Cu are preferred sites for proton adsorption and particularly active for H2 evolution. Thus, as the Cu edge atoms are replaced with indium having a high overpotential toward water reduction, H2 evolution is suppressed and instead CO2 reduction is facilitated.
Another important observation for CuIn alloy catalysts is the greatly enhanced CO selectivity induced by the electrochemical pre-activation, which causes formation of a surface In(OH)3 layer with oxygen vacancy as shown by XPS in Fig. 3d. In order to investigate directly the influence of the In(OH)3 layer, CuIn-Act was etched using 8M HCl and tested for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction in Fig. 5. The etched CuIn (CuIn-ActEtch) exhibits similar photocurrents, but a reduced CO selectivity relative to the original CuIn-Act. The high CO selectivity is completely recovered when the CuIn-Act-Etch is reactivated (CuIn-Act-Etch-Act), demonstrating the crucial role of In(OH)3 in CO selectivity. As studied in gas phase CO2 reduction over indium metal [20], oxygen-deficient indium and oxygen of indium hydroxide have slightly positive and negative charges to become Lewis acid and base, respectively, and they form a partial electric field on the surface [27,28]. By delivering electrons and protons, CO2 would be adsorbed and stabilized on the polarized surface as depicted in Fig. 6. Intermediate COOH* is formed by CO2 adsorption on oxygen deficient indium together with protons, and H2O* is generated on the In(OH)3 surface [29,30]. Then CO and H2O are easily desorbed with transferred electron. Thus, the amorphous In (OH)3 layer and oxygen vacancy improve faradaic efficiency to CO on the CuIn-Act catalyst.
In attempt to achieve highly efficient and selective CO2 to CO conversion, we have adopted the following strategies; 1) fabrication of 1-D nanowire electrocatalyst by anodization, 2) electrodeposition of In forming Cu-In alloy and 3) formation of In(OH)3 layer with oxygen vacancy on the CuIn alloy surface by the electrochemical pre-activation. The pre-activated Cu-In alloy gives a high current density (ca. −3.9mAcm−2 at −0.6 VRHE) and partial CO current density (ca. −2.66mAcm−2) with high CO selectivity (> 68.2%) and minor H2 evolution (< 11.7%) and HCOOH formation (< 5%), and demonstrates stable performance at least for 15 h. The results represent the great improvement by a factor of 4 over CuIn alloy powder electrocatalysts without nanostructuring.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
sections.text:
As mentioned, the challenges of electrochemical conversion of CO2 to CO in aqueous solution are low CO selectivity due to competitive CO2 and water reduction reactions, low reaction rates (or high overpotential) and high cost of electrocatalysts. Here we report 1-D CuIn nanowire alloy electrocatalyst having a thin overlayer of In(OH)3 with oxygen vacancy on the surface. The electrode exhibits the best performance in terms of the current density, CO selectivity and stability
among reported Cu-In based catalysts. The unique 1-D nanowire morphology offers a large surface area and facile charge transfer for the electrochemical CO2 reduction. Replacement of edge sites Cu atoms with indium in the CuIn alloy together with formation of an In(OH)3 surface layer with oxygen vacancy by electrochemical pre-activation promotes selective CO evolution suppressing competing H2 evolution.
